Pelf means money or wealth — but not just any money. It specifically refers to money that is viewed with moral disgust. Think of it as "dirty money." It's the kind of wealth associated with greed, dishonesty, corruption, or shameless self-interest. When someone uses the word "pelf," they are not just describing money — they are passing judgment on it. They are saying, in one sharp word, that this money is tainted and the pursuit of it is base and low.

So if regular money is neutral — just a tool — pelf is money with a sneer attached to it.

To really understand pelf, you need to understand its attitude. The word drips with contempt. It treats wealth as something shameful — something a morally decent person ought to be above chasing.

Imagine a greedy landlord who exploits his tenants, or a corrupt official who takes bribes, or a merchant who cheats his customers — the money they pile up? That's pelf. It's not just that the money was earned wrongly. The word can also be used more broadly to express contempt for the mere love of money — for people who put wealth above everything else: honor, kindness, integrity, relationships.

So pelf carries two layers:

  1. Money that was gained through greed or dishonest means.
  2. Money in general, when being described with moral contempt — as something corrupting, degrading, or unworthy of an honorable person.

Both layers are always present in the word's spirit, even if the first layer isn't always literally meant.
How It Differs from Similar Words

You might be thinking: don't words like "money," "riches," or "wealth" cover the same ground? They don't — and here's why.

"Money" and "wealth" are completely neutral. You can say "she earned a lot of money through hard work" and there's no judgment. You can't do that with pelf. Pelf is never neutral. It always judges.

The closest word in modern English is "lucre" — as in the famous phrase "filthy lucre." Lucre also means money, and also carries a negative moral tone. Pelf and lucre are siblings in that sense. But pelf is even more archaic and more emotionally loaded with contempt than lucre.
Who Uses This Word, and When

Pelf is an archaic word — meaning it was once in common use but is now largely old-fashioned. You won't hear someone say it in a casual conversation today. It belongs mostly to:

  • Old literature and poetry — especially from the 16th, 17th, and 18th centuries. Writers of that era used it freely when criticizing greed or corruption.
  • Modern writing for stylistic or rhetorical effect — a writer who wants to sound literary, or who wants to express a particularly sharp moral contempt for money and greed, might deliberately reach for "pelf."
  • Formal or elevated speech — occasionally used by someone who wishes to sound erudite while condemning someone's corrupt wealth.

If you encounter it in a novel, a poem, or a speech, it is almost certainly being used to condemn greed or dishonest gain.

These examples will show you exactly how the word behaves in real use:

  1. "He sacrificed his friends, his family, and his conscience — all for pelf."

Here, pelf emphasizes that the money he chased was not worth the moral cost. The word carries the judgment for you.

  1. "The politician preached virtue in public but secretly accumulated pelf through every corrupt scheme he could devise."

Here, pelf directly implies money gained through dishonesty and corruption.

  1. "She was a woman of principle who cared nothing for pelf."

Here, pelf is used more broadly — she didn't care about money in the grubby, all-consuming, morally compromising way that many people do. The word frames the love of money as something beneath her.

  1. "The temple had been turned into a marketplace for pelf, and it disgusted him."

Here, pelf is used to describe how sacred things were being traded for corrupt or ignoble gain.
The One Thing to Always Remember

If you remember nothing else, remember this: pelf is never a compliment, and it's never neutral. Every single time you see or hear this word, someone is expressing moral contempt — for money obtained through greed or dishonesty, or for the act of valuing money over everything that actually matters in a good human life.

It's a word of accusation dressed up as a noun.
